findings.claim: The hands-on activity prompts are short unnumbered task sentences; the page contains none of the mandated “Where to look / What to do or type / What to expect / How to know done” labels. Thus its activities do not provide the required numbered, observable completion path.

evidence.section: Labels or Instructions: provide labels or instructions when content requires user input

findings.recommendation: Rewrite every hands-on activity as numbered steps with the four mandated labels, without embedding reasoning answers. Preserve the current controls and feedback beneath those instructions.

findings.claim: The single Windows activation command .venv\Scripts\activate is presented as universal and is the keyed GIFT answer, but the official venv table gives different commands by shell: activate.bat for cmd.exe and Activate.ps1 for PowerShell. The current instruction can fail in the shell many Windows learners use.

evidence.section: How venvs work: platform- and shell-specific activation command table

findings.recommendation: Teach and quiz both Windows shells explicitly: .venv\Scripts\activate.bat in cmd.exe and .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 in PowerShell; keep source .venv/bin/activate for POSIX shells.

findings.claim: The asserted sys.path order—script folder, standard library, site-packages—is too absolute. Initialization can begin with the script directory or current directory, includes PYTHONPATH, prefix-dependent standard-library entries, and then site processing; -m, -c, isolated mode, environment variables, ._pth files, and sitecustomize change the path.

evidence.section: The initialization of the sys.path module search path

findings.recommendation: Label the three-entry diagram as the simplified normal case and add the omitted practical rule: import searches sys.path in order, whose initial entries depend on how Python starts and can be influenced by PYTHONPATH/site configuration. Avoid a universal three-step order in the quiz feedback.
